modern_osis:
Original heading

David's vow and profession of godliness.

A household and a kingdom governed under God

David declared how he intended to manage his household and his kingdom, resisting wrongdoing and encouraging godliness.

The psalm therefore applies to private families as well as rulers; it can be called the householder's psalm.

It teaches everyone who has authority, whether great or small, to use it so that evildoers are restrained and those who do right are encouraged.

David chose to sing of God's mercy and judgment.

The Lord's dealings with his people commonly include both.

He sets them beside each other, like rain and sunshine, for their good.

We should thank God appropriately for both his mercies and his judgments.

Family blessings and family afflictions alike should move us to maintain faithful worship at home.

Public responsibility never excuses neglect of one's household.

Indeed, those who hold public office have an even stronger duty to set a good example by governing their families well.

When someone has a home, that person should seek to have God dwelling there.

Those who walk faithfully, sincerely and uprightly may expect the Lord's presence.

David resolved first to refuse evil in his own conduct.

He also resolved not to surround himself with wicked servants or place ungodly people in positions of trust.

He did not want his household corrupted by their example.

A perverse and quarrelsome heart is destructive to fellowship, which is bound together by Christian love.

David would neither tolerate slanderers who delight in damaging their neighbors' reputations nor favor proud and deceitful people who lie or cheat without remorse.

Everyone should work diligently to reform their own heart and conduct, starting without delay.

Remember the coming day when the righteous King will remove evildoers from the heavenly Jerusalem.
classic_reading:
[Ps.101.1]
Chapter 101
David's vow and profession of godliness.
--In this psalm we have David declaring how he intended to regulate his household, and to govern his kingdom, that he might stop wickedness, and encourage godliness. It is also applicable to private families, and is the householder's psalm. It teaches all that have any power, whether more or less, to use it so as to be a terror to evil-doers, and a praise to them that do well. The chosen subject of the psalm is God's mercy and judgment. The Lord's providences concerning his people are commonly mixed; mercy and judgment. God has set the one over against the other, both to do good, like showers and sunshine. When, in his providence, he exercises us with the mixture of mercy and judgment, we must make suitable acknowledgments to him for both. Family mercies and family afflictions are both calls to family religion. Those who are in public stations are not thereby excused from care in governing their families; they are the more concerned to set a good example of ruling their own houses well. Whenever a man has a house of his own, let him seek to have God to dwell with him; and those may expect his presence, who walk with a perfect heart, in a perfect way. David resolves to practise no evil himself. He further resolves not to keep bad servants, nor to employ those about him that are wicked. He will not admit them into his family, lest they spread the infection of sin. A froward heart, one that delights to be cross and perverse, is not fit for society, the bond of which is Christian love. Nor will he countenance slanderers, those who take pleasure in wounding their neighbour's reputation. Also, God resists the proud, and false, deceitful people, who scruple not to tell lies, or commit frauds. Let every one be zealous and diligent to reform his own heart and ways, and to do this early; ever mindful of that future, most awful morning, when the King of righteousness shall cut off all wicked doers from the heavenly Jerusalem.

Giving sorrow a voice in prayer (verses 1–11)

All of God's word helps guide our prayers.

But in passages like this, the Holy Spirit places words directly in our mouths.

This prayer has been provided for afflicted people; let them bring it before God.

Even faithful believers can be nearly overwhelmed by trouble.

It is both our duty and our good to pray.

A suffering soul finds relief in humbly telling the Lord about its pain.

Still, we must say, Blessed be the Lord's name, whether he gives or takes away.

The psalmist viewed himself as nearing death, his days passing like a shadow.

Trusting the Lord's promises for his church (verses 12–22)

We are dying creatures, but God lives forever and continues to protect his church.

We can be confident that he will not neglect it.

When we consider our sinfulness, spiritual darkness, lifelessness and the many failings of our prayers, we may fear they will not be received in heaven.

But the gospel assures us otherwise.

We have an Advocate with the Father, and we live under grace rather than law.

Redemption is the subject of the Christian church's praise.

Israel's earthly rescue and restoration pictured that far greater work.

Lord Jesus, look upon us and bring us into the glorious freedom of your children, so that we may bless and praise your name.

The unchanging God and our passing lives (verses 23–28)

Illness can quickly weaken our strength and cut short the years we expected to have.

We should prepare for that possibility.

We must acknowledge God's hand in this and recognize that even an early death can be consistent with his love.

People who have used their strength faithfully sometimes grow weak.

Others whom we believe the world can hardly spare have their lives shortened.

Amid every change and danger facing the church, it is comforting to remember that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever.

When our bodies die or friends are taken from us, we may remember that God is everlasting.

Do not miss the assurance of a happy end to the believer's trials.

Everything else changes, wears out and perishes, like clothing being folded away.

Jesus lives forever.

Because he lives, the future of his people is secure.

He has promised, Because I live, you also will live.

Chapter 102
Chapter Outline
A sorrowful complaint of great afflictions. | (1-11) |
Encouragement by expecting the performances of God's promises to his church. | (12-22) |
The unchangeableness of God. | (23-28) |
Verses 1-11
The whole word of God is of use to direct us in prayer; but here, is often elsewhere, the Holy Ghost has put words into our mouths. Here is a prayer put into the hands of the afflicted; let them present it to God. Even good men may be almost overwhelmed with afflictions. It is our duty and interest to pray; and it is comfort to an afflicted spirit to unburden itself, by a humble representation of its griefs. We must say, Blessed be the name of the Lord, who both gives and takes away. The psalmist looked upon himself as a dying man; My days are like a shadow.
[Ps.102.12-Ps.102.22]
Verses 12-22
We are dying creatures, but God is an everlasting God, the protector of his church; we may be confident that it will not be neglected. When we consider our own vileness, our darkness and deadness, and the manifold defects in our prayers, we have cause to fear that they will not be received in heaven; but we are here assured of the contrary, for we have an Advocate with the Father, and are under grace, not under the law. Redemption is the subject of praise in the Christian church; and that great work is described by the temporal deliverance and restoration of Israel. Look down upon us, Lord Jesus; and bring us into the glorious liberty of thy children, that we may bless and praise thy name.
[Ps.102.23-Ps.102.28]
Verses 23-28
Bodily distempers soon weaken our strength, then what can we expect but that our months should be cut off in the midst; and what should we do but provide accordingly? We must own God's hand in it; and must reconcile this to his love, for often those that have used their strength well, have it weakened; and those who, as we think, can very ill be spared, have their days shortened. It is very comfortable, in reference to all the changes and dangers of the church, to remember that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever. And in reference to the death of our bodies, and the removal of friends, to remember that God is an everlasting God. Do not let us overlook the assurance this psalm contains of a happy end to all the believer's trials. Though all things are changing, dying, perishing, like a vesture folding up and hastening to decay, yet Jesus lives, and thus all is secure, for he hath said, Because I live ye shall live also.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesAn exhortation to bless God for his mercy.1–5And to the church and to all men.6–14For the constancy of his mercy.15–18For the government of the world.19–22
Bless the Lord for forgiveness and healing (verses 1–5)

When God forgives sin, he removes the obstacle that kept good things from us and restores us to his favor.

Think how much our sins have provoked him—yet they are pardoned.

So many provocations, yet all forgiven!

As we continue to sin and repent, God continues to forgive.

Because of Adam's fall, our bodies experience weakness and disease, and our souls suffer their own infirmities.

Christ alone forgives all our sins and heals all our infirmities.

The person who has experienced healing from the disease of sin has good reason to be assured of forgiveness.

When God's Spirit renews his people's weakened faith, granting grace, comfort, fresh life and joy as a pledge of eternal life, their strength seems restored like the vigor of youth (Job 33:25).

The compassion of our heavenly Father (verses 6–14)

God is good to all, but he has shown particular favor to Israel through revealing himself and his grace.

His ways include the commandments he calls us to obey, along with his promises and purposes.

He has always been full of compassion.

How unlike God are those who seize every excuse to rebuke someone and never know when to stop!

What would become of us if God treated us that way?

Scripture speaks constantly of his mercy, and we have all experienced it.

A father has compassion on his children in many situations.

When they lack understanding, he teaches.

When they are stubborn, he bears patiently.

When they are sick, he comforts.

When they fall, he helps them rise.

When they do wrong and submit, he forgives.

When they are wronged, he sets things right.

This is how the Lord takes pity on those who fear him.

He remembers how frail our bodies are and how foolish our souls can be.

He knows how little we can accomplish and how little we can endure.

His compassion takes account of all these limitations.

God's faithful mercy outlasts life (verses 15–18)

Human life is brief and uncertain.

A garden flower may last longer because its wall and gardener shelter it.

But a flower growing in an open field is exposed not only to its own decay, but also to cold weather and animals that may cut or trample it.

That is our condition.

God knows our frailty and has compassion on us.

We should remember it ourselves.

His mercy is better than life, because it will last longer than life.

His righteousness and his faithful promises remain blessings to children and grandchildren who follow their faithful ancestors in godliness.

The Lord reigns over everything (verses 19–22)

The One who made everything also rules everything, accomplishing both through his powerful word.

He directs people and events toward his glory.

Holy angels continually praise him.

Let all his works praise him.

Unceasingly delighting in God would have been natural to us if humanity had not fallen.

Through new birth, such delight begins to return.

In heaven it will be perfect forever.

We cannot be completely happy until we find unwearied joy in perfectly obeying God's will.

Let every redeemed heart say, Bless the Lord, O my soul!
classic_reading:
[Ps.103.1-Ps.103.5]
Chapter 103
Chapter Outline
An exhortation to bless God for his mercy. | (1-5) |
And to the church and to all men. | (6-14) |
For the constancy of his mercy. | (15-18) |
For the government of the world. | (19-22) |
Verses 1-5
By the pardon of sin, that is taken away which kept good things from us, and we are restored to the favor of God, who bestows good things on us. Think of the provocation; it was sin, and yet pardoned: how many the provocations, yet all pardoned! God is still forgiving, as we are still sinning and repenting. The body finds the melancholy consequences of Adam's offence, it is subject to many infirmities, and the soul also. Christ alone forgives all our sins; it is he alone who heals all our infirmities. And the person who finds his sin cured, has a well-grounded assurance that it is forgiven. When God, by the graces and comforts of his Spirit, recovers his people from their decays, and fills them with new life and joy, which is to them an earnest of eternal life and joy, they may then be said to return to the days of their youth, [Job.33.25] Job 33:25.
[Ps.103.6-Ps.103.14]
Verses 6-14
Truly God is good to all: he is in a special manner good to Israel. He has revealed himself and his grace to them. By his ways we may understand his precepts, the ways he requires us to walk in; and his promises and purposes. He always has been full of compassion. How unlike are those to God, who take every occasion to chide, and never know when to cease! What would become of us, if God should deal so with us? The Scripture says a great deal of the mercy of God, and we all have experienced it. The father pities his children that are weak in knowledge, and teaches them; pities them when they are froward, and bears with them; pities them when they are sick, and comforts them; pities them when they are fallen, and helps them to rise; pities them when they have offended, and, upon their submission, forgives them; pities them when wronged, and rights them: thus the Lord pities those that fear him. See why he pities. He considers the frailty of our bodies, and the folly of our souls, how little we can do, how little we can bear; in all which his compassion appears.
[Ps.103.15-Ps.103.18]
Verses 15-18
How short is man's life, and uncertain! The flower of the garden is commonly more choice, and will last the longer, for being sheltered by the garden-wall, and the gardener's care; but the flower of the field, to which life is here compared, is not only withering in itself, but exposed to the cold blasts, and liable to be cropt and trod on by the beasts of the field. Such is man. God considers this, and pities him; let him consider it himself. God's mercy is better than life, for it will outlive it. His righteousness, the truth of his promise, shall be unto children's children, who tread in the footsteps of their forefathers' piety. Then shall mercy be preserved to them.
[Ps.103.19-Ps.103.22]
Verses 19-22
He who made all, rules all, and both by a word of power. He disposes all persons and things to his own glory. There is a world of holy angels who are ever praising him. Let all his works praise him. Such would have been our constant delight, if we had not been fallen creatures. Such it will in a measure become, if we are born of God. Such it will be for ever in heaven; nor can we be perfectly happy till we can take unwearied pleasure in perfect obedience to the will of our God. And let the feeling of each redeemed heart be, Bless the Lord, O my soul.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod's majesty in the heavens, The creation of the sea, and the dry land.1–9His provision for all creatures.10–18The regular course of day and night, and God's sovereign power over all the creatures.19–30A resolution to continue praising God.31–35
The glory of the Creator (verses 1–9)

Everything we see calls us to praise and bless the Lord, who is great.

His eternal power and divine nature are evident in what he has made.

God is light, and there is no darkness in him.

The Lord Jesus, the beloved Son, is the Light of the world.

God's provision for every creature (verses 10–18)

As we consider the provision made for every living creature, we should notice how their existence offers natural praise to God.

Yet human beings, so forgetful and ungrateful, enjoy the largest share of their Creator's kindness.

Do not overlook the spiritual blessings pictured by these provisions: the fruitfulness of the church through grace, the bread of eternal life, the cup of salvation, and the oil of gladness.

If God provides for creatures of lesser strength and understanding, surely he will remain a refuge to his people.

Day, night, work, resurrection and Providence (verses 19–30)

Praise God for the continuing pattern of day and night.

People who wait for darkness in order to commit wicked acts resemble wild animals that emerge at night, keeping company with the fruitless works of darkness.

God hears the needs expressed by creatures according to their nature, including ravenous beasts.

How much more will he graciously understand the language of his own people, even weak, broken groanings that cannot be put into words?

Each day's work should be performed during the time given for it.

We should take up our responsibilities each morning and continue until evening.

Rest will come when night arrives, when no one can work.

The psalmist marvels at God's creation.

Human art often reveals roughness when examined closely.

But God's natural works appear even more detailed and orderly the closer we look.

Everything is made in wisdom, answering the purpose for which it was created.

Each spring suggests the resurrection, when new life seems to rise out of the ruin of the old world.

But unlike the other creatures described, human beings alone live beyond bodily death.

When God takes away breath, the soul enters another condition, and the body will rise again either to glory or misery.

May the Lord send his Spirit to make our souls new in holiness.

Creation's fading glory and the greater work of redemption (verses 31–35)

Human glory fades, while God's glory endures forever.

Creatures change, but their Creator never changes.

If contemplating the beauty of creation brings such delight to the soul, how much more wonderful is the work of redemption to an enlightened mind!

Only through that work can a sinner find sound grounds for confidence and joy in God.

He sustains everything with pleasure, governs everything and rejoices in his works.

May our souls, transformed by grace, keep reflecting upon him and praising his name.

[Ps.104.10-Ps.104.18]
Verses 10-18
When we reflect upon the provision made for all creatures, we should also notice the natural worship they render to God. Yet man, forgetful ungrateful man, enjoys the largest measure of his Creator's kindness. the earth, varying in different lands. Nor let us forget spiritual blessings; the fruitfulness of the church through grace, the bread of everlasting life, the cup of salvation, and the oil of gladness. Does God provide for the inferior creatures, and will he not be a refuge to his people?
[Ps.104.19-Ps.104.30]
Verses 19-30
We are to praise and magnify God for the constant succession of day and night. And see how those are like to the wild beasts, who wait for the twilight, and have fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness. Does God listen to the language of mere nature, even in ravenous creatures, and shall he not much more interpret favourably the language of grace in his own people, though weak and broken groanings which cannot be uttered? There is the work of every day, which is to be done in its day, which man must apply to every morning, and which he must continue in till evening; it will be time enough to rest when the night comes, in which no man can work. The psalmist wonders at the works of God. The works of art, the more closely they are looked upon, the more rough they appear; the works of nature appear more fine and exact. They are all made in wisdom, for they all answer the end they were designed to serve. Every spring is an emblem of the resurrection, when a new world rises, as it were, out of the ruins of the old one. But man alone lives beyond death. When the Lord takes away his breath, his soul enters on another state, and his body will be raised, either to glory or to misery. May the Lord send forth his Spirit, and new-create our souls to holiness.
[Ps.104.31-Ps.104.35]
Verses 31-35
Man's glory is fading; God's glory is everlasting: creatures change, but with the Creator there is no variableness. And if mediation on the glories of creation be so sweet to the soul, what greater glory appears to the enlightened mind, when contemplating the great work of redemption! There alone can a sinner perceive ground of confidence and joy in God. While he with pleasure upholds all, governs all, and rejoices in all his works, let our souls, touched by his grace, meditate on and praise him.

Seeking the Lord's strength and favor (verses 1–7)

This psalm calls us to stir ourselves up to praise God.

Seek his strength—meaning his grace, and the power of the Holy Spirit to accomplish in us the good we cannot do by ourselves.

That strength comes from him, and we must keep asking for it.

Seek his favor for eternity.

Continue seeking him throughout this life.

God will not only be found by those who seek him; he rewards those who diligently seek him.

God's covenant care and the story of Joseph (verses 8–23)

Remember the Redeemer's marvelous works, his wonders and the judgments he has spoken.

True believers may be few and live as strangers and pilgrims on earth.

Yet through God's covenant they have been promised an inheritance far greater than Canaan.

If the Holy Spirit has anointed them, nothing can ultimately harm them.

Even afflictions can be among their mercies.

They test faith and love, humble pride, loosen the hold of the world and make prayer more earnest.

Bread is called the staff of life because it supports the body.

When that support is taken away, the body weakens.

Likewise, God's word sustains the soul and is the bread of spiritual life.

Among the worst judgments is a famine of hearing the Lord's word.

Such a famine was severe in all lands when Christ appeared in the flesh.

Joseph's story pictures Christ's coming and its blessings.

At the appointed time, Christ was exalted as Mediator, holding all the treasures of grace and salvation.

Perishing sinners come to him and receive help.

Israel's deliverance as a picture of salvation (verses 24–45)

Believers often grow most in their souls when they carry the cross.

Likewise, the church may grow in true holiness and increase in number during persecution.

Yet God raises up instruments of deliverance, and persecutors may receive judgment.

See how he provided for Israel in the wilderness.

Every blessing given to Israel as a nation pictured spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus.

Christ has redeemed us by his blood, restored our souls toward holiness and freed us from Satan's bondage.

He guides and guards his people throughout their journey.

He feeds them with the bread of heaven and gives them the water of life from the Rock of salvation.

He will bring them safely to heaven.

He redeems them from iniquity and purifies them as his own people, eager to do good works.

[Ps.105.1-Ps.105.7]
Chapter 105
Chapter Outline
A solemn call to praise and serve the Lord. | (1-7) |
His gracious dealings with Israel. | (8-23) |
Their deliverance from Egypt, and their settlement in Canaan. | (24-45) |
Verses 1-7
Our devotion is here stirred up, that we may stir up ourselves to praise God. Seek his strength; that is, his grace; the strength of his Spirit to work in us that which is good, which we cannot do but by strength derived from him, for which he will be sought. Seek to have his favour to eternity, therefore continue seeking it while living in this world; for he will not only be found, but he will reward those that diligently seek him.
[Ps.105.8-Ps.105.23]
Verses 8-23
Let us remember the Redeemer's marvellous works, his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth. Though true Christians are few number, strangers and pilgrims upon earth, yet a far better inheritance than Canaan is made sure to them by the covenant of God; and if we have the anointing of the Holy Spirit, none can do us any harm. Afflictions are among our mercies. They prove our faith and love, they humble our pride, they wean us from the world, and quicken our prayers. Bread is the staff which supports life; when that staff is broken, the body fails and sinks to the earth. The word of God is the staff of spiritual life, the food and support of the soul: the sorest judgment is a famine of hearing the word of the Lord. Such a famine was sore in all lands when Christ appeared in the flesh; whose coming, and the blessed effect of it, are shadowed forth in the history of Joseph. At the appointed time Christ was exalted as Mediator; all the treasures of grace and salvation are at his disposal, perishing sinners come to him, and are relieved by him.
[Ps.105.24-Ps.105.45]
Verses 24-45
As the believer commonly thrives best in his soul when under the cross; so the church also flourishes most in true holiness, and increases in number, while under persecution. Yet instruments shall be raised up for their deliverance, and plagues may be expected by persecutors. And see the special care God took of his people in the wilderness. All the benefits bestowed on Israel as a nation, were shadows of spiritual blessings with which we are blessed in Christ Jesus. Having redeemed us with his blood, restored our souls to holiness, and set us at liberty from Satan's bondage, he guides and guards us all the way. He satisfies our souls with the bread of heaven, and the water of life from the Rock of salvation, and will bring us safely to heaven. He redeems his servants from all iniquity, and purifies them unto himself, to be a peculiar people, zealous of good works.

The joy of God's people (verses 1–5)

Neither our sins nor our sufferings should keep us from giving God glory and praise.

The less deserving we are, the more astonishing his kindness becomes.

Those who trust in the Redeemer's righteousness should try to follow his example, praising him by both word and action.

God's people have good reason for joy.

They have no need to envy the pleasures or pride of people who live only for this world.

Israel's sins and God's faithfulness (verses 6–12)

The psalm now turns to confession.

We must acknowledge that the Lord has acted rightly, while we have acted wickedly.

Though correction may be fully deserved, there is still hope that God will not abandon his people completely.

Even when suffering, they admit their guilt before him.

We begin to distrust the Lord when we forget his earlier mercies.

If God did not save us for his own name's sake, demonstrating his power and grace, all of us would perish.

Repeated rebellion and the hunger of the soul (verses 13–33)

Those who refuse to wait for God's counsel may justly be left to follow their own desires and schemes.

Excessive desire can become sinful even when the thing desired is lawful.

God showed his displeasure by filling them with uneasiness of mind, terror of conscience and painful self-reproach.

Some people eat lavishly every day and possess strong, healthy bodies, yet their souls are wasting away.

They have no love for God, no thankfulness and no appetite for the Bread of life.

Feeding the body while starving the soul is dreadful folly.

Even faithful believers have abundant reason to say that only the Lord's mercy has kept them from destruction.

We have often set up idols within our hearts, clinging to forbidden things.

Had One greater than Moses not stood to turn away the Lord's anger, we would have been destroyed.

God dealt severely even with Moses for rash words.

What, then, do people deserve when they frequently speak proudly and wickedly?

The Lord may justly take away relatives and others whose relationships have blessed us when we are irritable toward them, provoke them and grieve them.

Israel's failures in Canaan and the final appeal (verses 34–48)

Israel's conduct in Canaan and the Lord's dealings with the people teach that the path of sin runs downhill.

Neglecting a commanded duty opens the door to committing further sins.

The Israelites failed to drive out the pagan peoples and then learned their practices.

One sin led to many others and brought divine judgment.

In part, their sin became its own punishment.

Those who led sinners into evil may later become instruments of their ruin.

Satan first tempts and then torments.

Yet eventually God showed pity to his people for the sake of his covenant.

His unchanging compassion and faithful love led him to replace judgment with mercy.

Henry explains that when Scripture speaks of God's repenting, it does not mean a change in his merciful nature, but a change in how he deals with the people.

The condition of the visible church should sober us.

If Christian nations persist in grave sin, we should not be surprised when God humbles them.

Without widespread and deep repentance, they can expect further trouble.

The psalm closes with a prayer that the Lord will complete his people's deliverance and praise for what he has already begun to do.

May the entire world soon answer Amen.

God showed his displeasure for this. He filled them with uneasiness of mind, terror of conscience, and self-reproach. Many that fare deliciously every day, and whose bodies are healthful, have leanness in their souls: no love to God, no thankfulness, no appetite for the Bread of life, and then the soul must be lean. Those wretchedly forget themselves, that feast their bodies and starve their souls. Even the true believer will see abundant cause to say, It is of the Lord's mercies that I am not consumed. Often have we set up idols in our hearts, cleaved to some forbidden object; so that if a greater than Moses had not stood to turn away the anger of the Lord, we should have been destroyed. If God dealt severely with Moses for unadvised words, what do those deserve who speak many proud and wicked words? It is just in God to remove those relations that are blessings to us, when we are peevish and provoking to them, and grieve their spirits.
[Ps.106.34-Ps.106.48]
Verses 34-48
The conduct of the Israelites in Canaan, and God's dealings with them, show that the way of sin is down-hill; omissions make way for commissions: when they neglected to destroy the heathen, they learned their works. One sin led to many more, and brought the judgments of God on them. Their sin was, in part, their own punishment. Sinners often see themselves ruined by those who led them into evil. Satan, who is a tempter, will be a tormentor. At length, God showed pity to his people for his covenant's sake. The unchangeableness of God's merciful nature and love to his people, makes him change the course of justice into mercy; and no other change is meant by God's repentance. Our case is awful when the outward church is considered. When nations professing Christianity, are so guilty as we are, no wonder if the Lord brings them low for their sins. Unless there is general and deep repentance, there can be no prospect but of increasing calamities. The psalm concludes with prayer for completing the deliverance of God's people, and praise for the beginning and progress of it. May all the people of the earth, ere long, add their Amen.

God's help for travelers and exiles (verses 1–9)

These verses refer to Israel's deliverance from Egypt and perhaps also the return from Babylon, though the latter connection is uncertain.

They also describe the dangers experienced by travelers crossing the deserts of those lands.

It is difficult to imagine their suffering while wandering across featureless sand under the burning sun.

These travelers picture people whom the Lord has redeemed from Satan's bondage.

Believers pass through a world that can resemble a dangerous, desolate wilderness, sometimes fainting under trials, fears and temptations.

Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for God himself and for fellowship with him will be satisfied by the goodness of his house, now in grace and ultimately in glory.

God's mercy to prisoners (verses 10–16)

The prisoners described here are isolated and sorrowful.

Henry notes the severe treatment inflicted in eastern prisons.

Suffering should lead us toward humility.

If our hearts remain proud and unbroken through hardship, we lose an important benefit of the trial.

Earthly captivity pictures a sinner's rescue from a far worse imprisonment.

Once awakened to sin, a person recognizes guilt and misery.

After attempting in vain to secure freedom through personal effort, the sinner discovers that help can come only through God's mercy and grace.

The Lord forgives and breaks the power of sin and Satan, while the Holy Spirit brings sanctification and comfort.

Healing bodily and spiritual illness (verses 17–22)

Had humanity never sinned, sickness would not have entered the world.

Sinners behave foolishly when they damage their bodies through excess and endanger their lives by indulging uncontrolled appetites.

Such conduct is its own folly.

Illness weakens the body, but recovery comes through God's power and mercy.

We should thank him for every restoration of health.

Christ's miraculous healings also pictured his power to heal the diseases of the soul.

The Spirit of grace accomplishes such spiritual healing.

God sends his word to convict, convert and make people holy.

Even in ordinary bodily recovery, Providence operates at God's command.

Likewise, his word and Spirit restore the soul to spiritual health and holiness.

Deliverance from danger at sea (verses 23–32)

People who travel and work on the sea have special reason to reflect upon God's greatness.

Sailors witness terrible storms and extraordinary rescues that others can barely imagine.

How appropriate it is to pray during such danger!

Storms at sea also picture the terrors of a troubled conscience and the painful experiences some Christians endure.

When they cry to the Lord, he can turn their storm into calm and bring their trials to an end with joy.

Recognizing God's providence in changing fortunes (verses 33–43)

Human circumstances change in surprising ways.

The desolate condition of Judea and other lands offered illustrations to Henry's readers.

People may grow from humble beginnings to prosperity, yet fall from that success into nothing just as quickly.

Worldly riches are uncertain.

Those who possess them may suddenly lose them.

God has many ways of making people poor.

The righteous have reason to rejoice.

Such reversals will eventually silence those who deny divine Providence.

Sinners who see God justly taking away blessings they abused will have no valid defense.

We greatly benefit from recognizing God's goodness and allowing it to affect our hearts.

Wisdom calls us to perform our duty and leave our comfort to him.

A genuinely wise person will treasure this psalm and learn from it both human weakness and misery and God's power and lovingkindness—shown not because we deserve them but because he is merciful.

In captivity. | (10-16) |

God's hand is to be seen by his own people. | (33-43) |
Verses 1-9
In these verses there is reference to the deliverance from Egypt, and perhaps that from Babylon: but the circumstances of travellers in those countries are also noted. It is scarcely possible to conceive the horrors suffered by the hapless traveller, when crossing the trackless sands, exposed to the burning rays of the sum. The words describe their case whom the Lord has redeemed from the bondage of Satan; who pass through the world as a dangerous and dreary wilderness, often ready to faint through troubles, fears, and temptations. Those who hunger and thirst after righteousness, after God, and communion with him, shall be filled with the goodness of his house, both in grace and glory.
[Ps.107.10-Ps.107.16]
Verses 10-16
This description of prisoners and captives intimates that they are desolate and sorrowful. In the eastern prisons the captives were and are treated with much severity. Afflicting providences must be improved as humbling providences; and we lose the benefit, if our hearts are unhumbled and unbroken under them. This is a shadow of the sinner's deliverance from a far worse confinement. The awakened sinner discovers his guilt and misery. Having struggled in vain for deliverance, he finds there is no help for him but in the mercy and grace of God. His sin is forgiven by a merciful God, and his pardon is accompanied by deliverance from the power of sin and Satan, and by the sanctifying and comforting influences of God the Holy Spirit.
[Ps.107.17-Ps.107.22]
Verses 17-22
If we knew no sin, we should know no sickness. Sinners are fools. They hurt their bodily health by intemperance, and endanger their lives by indulging their appetites. This their way is their folly. The weakness of the body is the effect of sickness. It is by the power and mercy of God that we are recovered from sickness, and it is our duty to be thankful. All Christ's miraculous cures were emblems of his healing diseases of the soul. It is also to be applied to the spiritual cures which the Spirit of grace works. He sends his word, and heals souls; convinces, converts them, makes them holy, and all by the word. Even in common cases of recovery from sickness, God in his providence speaks, and it is done; by his word and Spirit the soul is restored to health and holiness.
[Ps.107.23-Ps.107.32]
Verses 23-32
Let those who go to sea, consider and adore the Lord. Mariners have their business upon the tempestuous ocean, and there witness deliverances of which others cannot form an idea. How seasonable it is at such a time to pray! This may remind us of the terrors and distress of conscience many experience, and of those deep scenes of trouble which many pass through, in their Christian course. Yet, in answer to their cries, the Lord turns their storm into a calm, and causes their trials to end in gladness.
[Ps.107.33-Ps.107.43]
Verses 33-43
What surprising changes are often made in the affairs of men! Let the present desolate state of Judea, and of other countries, explain this. If we look abroad in the world, we see many greatly increase, whose beginning was small. We see many who have thus suddenly risen, as suddenly brought to nothing. Worldly wealth is uncertain; often those who are filled with it, ere they are aware, lose it again. God has many ways of making men poor. The righteous shall rejoice. It shall fully convince all those who deny the Divine Providence. When sinners see how justly God takes away the gifts they have abused, they will not have a word to say. It is of great use to us to be fully assured of God's goodness, and duly affected with it. It is our wisdom to mind our duty, and to refer our comfort to him. A truly wise person will treasure in his heart this delightful psalm. From it, he will fully understand the weakness and wretchedness of man, and the power and loving-kindness of God, not for our merit, but for his mercy's sake.

Praise, faith and confidence in God's help

We can help our worship by selecting passages from different psalms, as this psalm does from Psalms 57 and 60.

Such passages can strengthen devotion and awaken gratitude.

When the heart is steadfast in faith and love, the tongue brings honor to its owner by speaking and singing God's praise.

Every gift received from the Lord benefits and honors the person who receives it when it is used in God's service and for his glory.

Believers can pray with confident faith and hope for every blessing of salvation.

These blessings are guaranteed by God's faithful covenant and promise.

They may therefore expect God's help in every trouble and victory in every conflict.

Whatever we accomplish or obtain, God must receive all the glory.

Lord, visit all our souls with this salvation and with the favor you show your chosen people.
classic_reading:
Chapter 108
--We may usefully select passages from different psalms, as here, Psa 57; 60, to help our devotions, and enliven our gratitude. When the heart is firm in faith and love, the tongue, being employed in grateful praises, is our glory. Every gift of the Lord honours and profits the possessor, as it is employed in God's service and to his glory. Believers may pray with assured faith and hope, for all the blessings of salvation; which are secured to them by the faithful promise and covenant of God. Then let them expect from him help in every trouble, and victory in every conflict. Whatever we do, whatever we gain, God must have all the glory. Lord, visit all our souls with this salvation, with this favour which thou bearest to thy chosen people.

Turning to God when enemies accuse us (verses 1–5)

It is an inexpressible comfort to believers that God is for them, whatever enemies oppose them.

They may appeal to him with confidence because he willingly cares for their cause.

David's enemies ridiculed his devotion, but they could not make him abandon it.

A prophetic warning of judgment (verses 6–20)

Henry understands these denunciations as words that the Lord Jesus may speak in his role as Judge, announcing the sentence awaiting certain enemies in order to warn others.

When people reject Christ's salvation, even their prayers may become sinful.

What leads some people to shameful deaths and causes others' families and property to collapse?

What brings disgrace, poverty, misery and ruin upon their descendants, making them and their families despised and hateful to others?

Sin—that destructive and poisonous evil—is the source of such devastation.

Consider the effect of the final sentence “Go, you cursed” upon the bodies and souls of the unrepentant.

What fear, pain, horror, anguish and despair it brings!

Sinners, take these warnings seriously: tremble and repent.

Praying for mercy and trusting the risen Advocate (verses 21–31)

The psalmist appealed to God's comfort in great humility.

He was distressed in mind.

His body had grown thin and weak.

Yet it is better to have a weak body with a spiritually healthy soul than to feast the body while starving the soul.

He was mocked and insulted by his enemies.

But if God blesses us, we need not fear human curses.

People cannot place a curse upon those whom God has chosen to bless.

The psalmist pleaded for God's glory and the honor of his name.

Save me, Lord—not because I deserve it, for I claim no merit—but because of your mercy.

He ended with the joyful confidence of faith, convinced his present struggle would end in victory.

Everyone who suffers according to God's will should commit their souls to his care.

Jesus, unjustly put to death and now risen, is the Advocate and Intercessor of his people.

He is always ready to appear on their behalf against a corrupt world and the great accuser.

Verses 1-5
It is the unspeakable comfort of all believers, that whoever is against them, God is for them; and to him they may apply as to one pleased to concern himself for them. David's enemies laughed at him for his devotion, but they could not laugh him out of it.
[Ps.109.6-Ps.109.20]
Verses 6-20
The Lord Jesus may speak here as a Judge, denouncing sentence on some of his enemies, to warn others. When men reject the salvation of Christ, even their prayers are numbered among their sins. See what hurries some to shameful deaths, and brings the families and estates of others to ruin; makes them and theirs despicable and hateful, and brings poverty, shame, and misery upon their posterity: it is sin, that mischievous, destructive thing. And what will be the effect of the sentence, "Go, ye cursed," upon the bodies and souls of the wicked! How it will affect the senses of the body, and the powers of the soul, with pain, anguish, horror, and despair! Think on these things, sinners, tremble and repent.
[Ps.109.21-Ps.109.31]
Verses 21-31
The psalmist takes God's comforts to himself, but in a very humble manner. He was troubled in mind. His body was wasted, and almost worn away. But it is better to have leanness in the body, while the soul prospers and is in health, than to have leanness in the soul, while the body is feasted. He was ridiculed and reproached by his enemies. But if God bless us, we need not care who curses us; for how can they curse whom God has not cursed; nay, whom he has blessed? He pleads God's glory, and the honour of his name. Save me, not according to my merit, for I pretend to none, but according to thy-mercy. He concludes with the joy of faith, in assurance that his present conflicts would end in triumphs. Let all that suffer according to the will of God, commit the keeping of their souls to him. Jesus, unjustly put to death, and now risen again, is an Advocate and Intercessor for his people, ever ready to appear on their behalf against a corrupt world, and the great accuser.

Original heading

Christ's kingdom.

The eternal King and Priest

This psalm speaks glorious truths concerning Jesus Christ.

He is not only greater than all the rulers of the earth.

He already existed in glory as the eternal Son of God.

Christ sits at God's right hand.

Sitting is a posture of rest after labor and suffering, and one from which the King exercises judgment and authority.

It also signifies permanence: he reigns forever.

All his enemies are already in chains, though they have not yet been made his footstool.

His kingdom has been established and will continue despite every power of darkness.

Christ's people are willing people.

The Holy Spirit's power makes them willing to serve him.

They worship him clothed with the beauty of holiness, which belongs to his house forever.

Many will dedicate themselves to him.

We should consecrate even the earliest days of our youth to the Lord Jesus, like fresh dew appearing at dawn.

Christ is not only King but also Priest.

He serves on God's behalf toward us and pleads our cause before the Father.

He is therefore the Mediator between God and humanity.

His priesthood follows the order of Melchizedek, earlier than Aaron's priesthood and superior to it in several ways.

It represents the priesthood of Christ more fully.

His place at God's right hand brings joy to his people and terror to his enemies.

Ultimately his victory will bring the final overthrow of those who oppose him.

The Redeemer saves and comforts his friends.

He was humbled, drinking from the stream along his path.

Henry understands this as a possible picture of the curse of the law and the wrath associated with our redemption, which Christ endured.

He drank the waters of suffering on the road toward his throne of glory.

He was humbled, but now he is exalted.

What about us?

Has Christ's gospel become God's saving power in our lives?

Does he reign in our hearts?

Are we willing subjects?

We once did not recognize our need for his salvation and resisted his rule.

Are we now willing to abandon every sin, turn away from an evil and deceptive world, and rest only upon his merit and mercy?

Do we welcome him as Prophet, Priest and King, and desire holiness?

Those transformed in this way receive the blessings of his sacrifice, intercession and grace.
classic_reading:
[Ps.110.1]
Chapter 110
Christ's kingdom.
--Glorious things are here spoken of Christ. Not only he should be superior to all the kings of the earth, but he then existed in glory as the eternal Son of God. Sitting is a resting posture: after services and sufferings, to give law, to give judgment. It is a remaining posture: he sits like a king for ever. All his enemies are now in a chain, but not yet made his footstool. And his kingdom, being set up, shall be kept up in the world, in despite of all the powers of darkness. Christ's people are a willing people. The power of the Spirit, going with the power of the world, to the people of Christs, is effectual to make them willing. They shall attend him in the beautiful attire of holiness; which becomes his house for ever. And he shall have many devoted to him. The dew of our youth, even in the morning of our days, ought to be consecrated to our Lord Jesus. Christ shall not only be a King, but a Priest. He is God's Minister to us, and our Advocate with the Father, and so is the Mediator between God and man. He is a Priest of the order of Melchizedek, which was before that of Aaron, and on many accounts superior to it, and a more lively representation of Christ's priesthood. Christ's sitting at the right hand of God, speaks as much terror to his enemies as happiness to his people. The effect of this victory shall be the utter ruin of his enemies. We have here the Redeemer saving his friends, and comforting them. He shall be humbled; he shall drink of the brook in the way. The wrath of God, running in the curse of the law, may be considered as the brook in the way of his undertaking. Christ drank of the waters of affliction in his way to the throne of glory. But he shall be exalted. What then are we? Has the gospel of Christ been to us the power of God unto salvation? Has his kingdom been set up in our hearts? Are we his willing subjects? Once we knew not our need of his salvation, and we were not willing that he should reign over us. Are we willing to give up every sin, to turn from a wicked, insnaring world, and rely only on his merits and mercy, to have him for our Prophet, Priest, and King? and do we desire to be holy? To those who are thus changed, the Saviour's sacrifice, intercession, and blessing belong.
